rules.title: Define shared constants when needed
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: A meaningful app-wide value is shared or repeated
rules.rule: Do not create a constants container speculatively; define genuinely shared values once as static properties on a purpose-named enum, keeping Feature-specific values with their owner.
rules.why: A single definition avoids inconsistent copies while keeping related code easy to find.
rules.verify: Check repeated uses, ownership, bundle metadata, localization and that no secrets are embedded.
rules.example: An AppLinks enum holds the shared company website and support email address.

rules.title: Keep the project structure understandable
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating or restructuring a CFA app
rules.rule: Group Views and ViewModels separately from AppModel, Features and their services; retain actual Xcode target membership.
rules.why: Developers can locate capability ownership without following arbitrary layers.
rules.verify: Inspect folders, target membership, resource paths and build configuration.
rules.example: Place NotesView and NotesViewModel together in the View layer, and NotesFeature in the Model layer.

rules.title: Keep business decisions in the Model
rules.section: Maintain an Absolute UI and Model Boundary
rules.applies: Creating or changing UI
rules.rule: Views render and forward intent; Features own domain decisions and authoritative state.
rules.why: A different device can reuse the same business capability.
rules.verify: Trace validation, calculations and persistence from the screen to their model owner.
rules.example: A weight screen sends a save request to its Feature; the Feature validates and persists the value.

rules.title: Each screen owns its ViewModel
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Creating or reviewing a SwiftUI screen
rules.rule: A screen creates and retains its own private ViewModel; do not pass or share ViewModels between Views.
rules.why: Presentation state remains local to the screen.
rules.verify: Inspect screen declarations, navigation destinations, previews and ViewModel construction.
rules.example: NotesView declares its own private State-backed NotesViewModel.

rules.title: Pass selected values to detail screens
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: A destination needs a selected item
rules.rule: A detail View may receive a selected immutable snapshot and use it to construct its own State-backed ViewModel in the View initializer.
rules.why: Each destination can preserve its selection independently.
rules.verify: Test two independently selected destinations and confirm refresh does not silently replace a displayed snapshot.
rules.example: Next Rocket Launch passes a selected snapshot into its [detail View](https://github.com/3DaysOfSwift/RocketLaunch-iOS-App-Swift-Concurrency/blob/3ecaa30c76428bd8a6f5db8fd5506b6c20b846f7/Swift%20Concurrency%20Project/RocketLaunch/1%20-%20View/Views/Operators/LaunchDetail/LaunchDetailView.swift) and its [ViewModel](https://github.com/3DaysOfSwift/RocketLaunch-iOS-App-Swift-Concurrency/blob/3ecaa30c76428bd8a6f5db8fd5506b6c20b846f7/Swift%20Concurrency%20Project/RocketLaunch/1%20-%20View/Views/Operators/LaunchDetail/LaunchDetailViewModel.swift).

rules.title: Keep view construction and edits local
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Creating screens and editing saved values
rules.rule: Keep View initializers free of I/O and work; the screen ViewModel owns unsaved text-field values until a save succeeds or the user cancels; retain the draft after a failed save.
rules.why: Screen creation remains predictable and cancelled edits do not change authoritative state.
rules.verify: Inspect initialization and test failed saves, retry and cancellation.
rules.example: An unsaved weight field remains on screen after a failed save and is discarded by Cancel.

rules.title: Define Features by capability
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: Identifying domain ownership
rules.rule: Features represent business capabilities and own authoritative application state; do not generate a Feature simply for each screen.
rules.why: A Feature can serve multiple screens or targets.
rules.verify: Map actual capabilities and state owners; check that screens consume the Features they need.
rules.example: A Settings screen can use SettingsFeature and UserProfileFeature without creating a Feature just for the screen.

rules.title: Compose Features only for real workflows
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: A business workflow genuinely spans Features
rules.rule: Prefer independent Features; an existing Feature or distinct coordinating Feature can coordinate other Features when a real business responsibility requires it.
rules.why: Avoid both feature spaghetti and needless coordinators.
rules.verify: Trace the workflow, verify one owner per state and check dependencies for cycles.
rules.example: A Today capability can coordinate existing Features when its reusable selection decisions belong in the Model.

rules.title: Coordinate account changes explicitly
rules.section: Define Features by Business Capability, Not by Screen or Tab
rules.applies: Sign-out, account switching or session expiration affects other Features
rules.rule: UserProfileFeature may call affected Features directly; if sign-out fails before the session ends, retain the session and account data. After success clear affected state and prevent stale requests republishing old data.
rules.why: A visible direct workflow avoids unnecessary event infrastructure while protecting account data.
rules.verify: Test failed and successful sign-out, account switch, in-flight requests and partial authentication outcomes.
rules.example: After successful sign-out, UserProfileFeature asks OrdersFeature and FavouritesFeature to clear account data.

rules.title: Compose the application model once per process
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Composing a CFA app or target
rules.rule: AppModel constructs and exposes concrete Features through an explicit graph and contains no UI navigation or Feature business rules.
rules.why: The Model has one visible entry point within each process.
rules.verify: Review live composition, initializer dependencies and isolated test graphs.
rules.example: In [NotesReference.swift](../examples/NotesReference.swift), AppModel.live() constructs NotesFeature and its storage dependency for the application graph.

rules.title: Own application-wide listeners at AppModel
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: An event must be observed independent of a screen
rules.rule: AppModel owns app-wide listener tasks and forwards events to the responsible Feature; screen-only observation stays with its screen or ViewModel.
rules.why: Lifetime follows the scope that requires the event.
rules.verify: Verify listener startup, event forwarding, lifetime, cancellation and test isolation.
rules.example: AppModel owns an app-wide purchase event listener and forwards updates to PurchasesFeature.

rules.title: Share Model code across device targets
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Adding a widget or another device target
rules.rule: Include shared Model source and target-specific Views and ViewModels; each process has its own AppModel and Features.
rules.why: Capabilities can be reused without assuming shared process memory.
rules.verify: Build each target, verify API availability and test snapshot transfer and updates.
rules.example: An iPhone widget reads a shared App Group snapshot; a Watch receives a copy through Watch Connectivity.

rules.title: Preserve deferred destinations
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Handling deep links or notification destinations
rules.rule: For new apps, DeepLinkingFeature records requests to open a URL or notification action, not scheduled or merely delivered notifications. The receiving scene owns navigation; either scene can open a shared pending request. Remove it after successful navigation or explicit dismissal. Preserve existing history during migration.
rules.why: The user can keep editing without losing the destination.
rules.verify: Test request reception, durable restoration, refusal, successful navigation, multiple requests, storage failure and scene isolation.
rules.example: A launch notification remains pending when a user chooses to keep editing; opening its page removes the request.

rules.title: Keep microservices small and well placed
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Choosing or sharing lower-level services
rules.rule: Keep a service with its Feature while ownership remains descriptive; place generic services in a shared location when justified.
rules.why: Organizing code around capability makes it easier to find.
rules.verify: Inspect actual service users, mutable state, dependency injection and responsibilities.
rules.example: A launch-specific provider can stay in the schedule folder; a generic network wrapper may move to shared services.

rules.title: Let independent requests progress
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Designing network services
rules.strength: Required unless a documented policy limits concurrency
rules.rule: Prefer a simple stateless NetworkingManager when suitable; do not assume an actor serializes an entire suspended request.
rules.why: Avoid accidental bottlenecks and data races.
rules.verify: Test overlapping requests and inspect isolation, request limits and URLSession configuration.
rules.example: Independent launch providers initiate requests without waiting for another provider to finish.

rules.title: Publish durable edits after saving
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Saving a user edit or other durable command
rules.rule: Publish confirmed saved state only after required authoritative persistence succeeds; preserve input on failure.
rules.why: The UI must not claim that an unsaved change was saved.
rules.verify: Inject failed and successful writes; check state and retry behaviour.
rules.example: A failed weight save leaves the saved collection unchanged and retains the entered value for retry.

rules.title: Use optional snapshots without blocking fresh data
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Caching replaceable server data
rules.strength: Required when using this cache pattern
rules.rule: Start restoration and refresh independently where both are needed; a successful current response does not wait for an optional cache write and must not be overwritten by an older snapshot.
rules.why: Previously downloaded data can appear quickly without sacrificing fresher server data.
rules.verify: Test missing, corrupt, slow and failed cache operations and out-of-order completion.
rules.example: A schedule refresh publishes new server data even if its optional snapshot write is slow or fails.

rules.title: Choose synchronization to match the product
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: An app requires cross-device data or offline edits
rules.rule: Do not add offline editing by default; prefer suitable system-managed sync, and use a dedicated server sync solution only when needed.
rules.why: The simplest storage strategy depends on actual product requirements.
rules.verify: Verify capabilities, schema, failure, retry and conflict behaviour on supported devices.
rules.example: SwiftData with CloudKit may suit a compatible Apple-device app; a server-backed app follows its server contract.

rules.title: Define task ownership and overlapping-call policy
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Starting asynchronous operations
rules.rule: Each Feature defines whether equivalent calls share execution or commands queue, and owns work that must outlive a screen.
rules.why: Task lifetime and repeated actions remain predictable.
rules.verify: Test overlapping callers, cancellation, failure, stale results and operation cleanup.
rules.example: Two equivalent refresh callers await the same Feature-owned request.

rules.title: Keep shared refreshes alive across navigation
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: A screen leaves during a Feature-owned refresh
rules.rule: Continue the shared refresh and retain successful data even when the screen that requested it leaves; later equivalent callers can join.
rules.why: The user may return and benefit from completed work.
rules.verify: Cancel the screen waiter and verify the request and another caller remain correct.
rules.example: A schedule refresh continues after the user leaves the screen and its result is available on return.

rules.title: Start the model synchronously
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Handling app launch
rules.rule: The app delegate calls AppModel startup synchronously; Features start asynchronous work without blocking launch on disk or network.
rules.why: App-wide startup signals are issued before the delegate returns.
rules.verify: Inspect the launch callback, repeated launch guard and first-frame behaviour.
rules.example: The application delegate calls AppModel startup directly; Features start their own asynchronous refreshes.

rules.title: Feature-owned background capabilities
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Registering iOS background work
rules.rule: Features own their domain work and may register handlers synchronously during app startup; route system callbacks and satisfy expiration and completion contracts.
rules.why: System lifecycle handling stays separate from feature behaviour.
rules.verify: Verify task identifiers, launch registration, expiration, completion and actual device behaviour.
rules.example: AppModel asks a Feature to register an eligible system background handler during launch.

rules.title: Observe authoritative state
rules.section: Use Observation Deliberately
rules.applies: Displaying shared model data
rules.rule: Expose observable Feature state while retaining a single owner; observation alone does not synchronize independent devices or processes.
rules.why: Views can update without creating competing domain state.
rules.verify: Trace the observed property from its Feature owner to the displayed View.
rules.example: A View reads an observable Feature value and updates when that value changes.

rules.title: Check paid capability entry points
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: A product marks a capability paid
rules.rule: PurchasesFeature owns entitlement state; the screen ViewModel checks it before presenting or calling the capability. Check every relevant entry point, including other callers. A server protects its own operations.
rules.why: Pricing changes remain separate from capability behaviour.
rules.verify: Trace every known paid entry point and test locked and entitled outcomes.
rules.example: An export screen checks PurchasesFeature before presenting or calling the paid export capability.

rules.title: Test architecture at its boundaries
rules.section: Test the Same Boundaries the Architecture Advertises
rules.applies: Implementing or changing CFA behaviour
rules.rule: Test observable behaviour with isolated Feature dependencies and real ownership boundaries.
rules.why: Tests establish behaviour rather than reproduce implementation details.
rules.verify: Run relevant tests and builds; state what was not executed.
rules.example: A Feature test injects a failing storage dependency and verifies that the saved value stays unchanged.

rules.title: Preserve product intent
rules.section: Architecture versus product design
rules.applies: Creating, migrating or maintaining an app
rules.rule: Preserve business outcomes and capabilities while migrating to CFA and Swift Concurrency; fix confirmed in-scope defects and allow necessary minor platform-driven presentation differences without seeking unrelated modernisation.
rules.why: Migration changes how the app works internally without silently removing what users rely on.
rules.verify: Compare the requested journey and business outcomes; test defect fixes and document material platform-driven differences.
rules.example: A migration retains the purchase flow, corrects an in-scope verified defect, and accepts a minor tab bar appearance change required by the platform.

rules.title: Respect project identity
rules.section: Project Identity
rules.applies: Creating or adapting an Xcode project
rules.rule: Follow the project identity rules and user-specified bundle identifier; never change existing identifiers merely to match an example.
rules.why: Identifiers control signing, capabilities and published app continuity.
rules.example: A new target derives its bundle identifier from the product name and requested prefix.
rules.verify: Inspect all build configurations and the built app metadata.

rules.title: Maintain template and resource membership
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Editing project layout or templates
rules.rule: Preserve the Xcode template layout contract, resource lookup and target membership.
rules.why: A correct folder tree is not sufficient if Xcode does not compile or bundle the files.
rules.example: A migrated Feature is moved into its proper folder and retained in the intended target.
rules.verify: Inspect the project and build all affected targets.

rules.title: Keep presentation state out of Features
rules.section: Maintain an Absolute UI and Model Boundary
rules.applies: Implementing navigation or display interactions
rules.rule: Keep screen-specific presentation, focus, selection and navigation within the presentation layer.
rules.why: Multiple scenes can present the same model independently.
rules.example: Two launch detail screens retain different selected snapshots.
rules.verify: Review independent windows and navigation while shared data updates.

rules.title: Publish immutable domain snapshots
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Exposing API or persistence data as domain values
rules.rule: Use let properties for published snapshot structs and construct replacement values after confirmed changes.
rules.why: A copy should not diverge by being mutated as though it were authoritative.
rules.example: A new launch value replaces an earlier snapshot after a successful refresh.
rules.verify: Inspect published value types and ensure callers use Feature commands to change durable data.

rules.title: Keep one authoritative Feature owner
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: Managing shared application state
rules.rule: A single MainActor Feature owns each piece of authoritative shared application state; lower services may own implementation machinery.
rules.why: Callers can identify which component decides the current business state.
rules.example: WeightLogFeature owns saved weight entries while a storage service handles persistence.
rules.verify: Trace reads and writes through all screens and services and check for competing authorities.

rules.title: Avoid an application-wide ViewModel
rules.section: Use AppModel as the Composition Root and Feature Facade
rules.applies: Composing the presentation layer
rules.rule: Keep ViewModels owned by their screens and out of AppModel.
rules.why: AppModel exposes model capabilities without owning UI state.
rules.example: Each screen creates a ViewModel that accesses the required concrete Features.
rules.verify: Inspect AppModel properties and the ViewModel ownership tree.

rules.title: Use MainActor for Features
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Defining a CFA Feature
rules.rule: Isolate Feature owners to MainActor; give underlying work an appropriate isolation strategy and avoid expensive blocking work on MainActor.
rules.why: Observable state is coordinated while substantial processing remains responsive.
rules.example: A Feature publishes a decoded schedule returned by a suitably isolated provider.
rules.verify: Inspect isolation annotations and run responsiveness checks where appropriate.

rules.title: Check suspension and stale results
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Updating state across async suspension
rules.rule: Treat await as a possible suspension and check that the operation is still entitled to publish its result.
rules.why: Actor isolation does not make an entire async workflow atomic.
rules.example: An earlier search cannot overwrite a newer query result.
rules.verify: Force out-of-order results and cancellation in controlled tests.

rules.title: Use cancellation to match the work
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: Designing task lifetime
rules.rule: Define cancellation at the operation boundary; cancel obsolete presentation work while preserving independent shared and durable work.
rules.why: Leaving one screen should not accidentally abandon work needed elsewhere.
rules.example: A superseded search stops while a shared refresh continues.
rules.verify: Test a cancelled waiter, a later caller and stale completion.

rules.title: Restore safe defaults for obsolete preferences
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Restoring a non-critical preference
rules.rule: Use a product-defined safe fallback for a missing or obsolete recognized value; distinguish storage corruption and failed writes.
rules.why: An old theme should not force the user to solve an internal compatibility issue.
rules.example: An unavailable saved colour theme falls back to system appearance.
rules.verify: Test a known preference, an obsolete value and a genuine storage error.

rules.title: Keep scene navigation independent
rules.section: Keep Screen Initializers Clean
rules.applies: Opening a link or notification in a multi-window app
rules.rule: Route each destination through a scene-appropriate handler without putting scene navigation state inside DeepLinkingFeature.
rules.why: A link should not unexpectedly redirect another window.
rules.example: A Settings screen asks the Feature to open its pending item in the receiving scene.
rules.verify: Test two scenes, declined navigation and unavailable destination handling.

rules.title: Keep unsaved field edits in the ViewModel
rules.section: Preserve One Authoritative Owner for Shared State
rules.applies: Editing a simple text field
rules.rule: Keep the unsaved field value in the screen ViewModel until a save succeeds or the user cancels; retain it after a failed save. Persisted values remain Feature-owned.
rules.why: An abandoned edit does not become shared application state.
rules.example: A weight editor keeps the entered number after a failed save.
rules.verify: Exercise save, failure, retry and Cancel without mutating the Feature early.

rules.title: Inject volatile dependencies
rules.section: Keep Time and Other Volatile Dependencies Injectable
rules.applies: Business decisions depend on time or another changing external value
rules.rule: Supply volatile dependencies in a controllable form rather than hiding them in business decisions.
rules.why: Time-dependent behaviour can be reproduced in tests.
rules.example: A countdown decision uses an injected clock.
rules.verify: Test boundary dates and time zones using controlled inputs.

rules.title: Use readable Feature commands
rules.section: Organize Behaviour into Cohesive Features
rules.applies: Designing a Feature API
rules.rule: Expose domain-oriented operations and values instead of deep storage graphs or generic mechanics.
rules.why: Callers can understand what a capability does from its API.
rules.example: A weight Feature exposes a named operation to save an entry.
rules.verify: Read call sites and check they do not manipulate repositories or nested implementation state.

rules.title: Prefer straightforward change
rules.section: Prefer Readable Domain Language over Architectural Ceremony
rules.applies: Implementing or migrating code
rules.rule: Choose the simplest structure that preserves necessary behaviour, ownership and safety.
rules.why: Fewer unnecessary layers improve comprehension and maintenance.
rules.example: A sign-out workflow uses direct Feature calls instead of a new event bus.
rules.verify: Trace the whole workflow and remove scaffolding with no demonstrated purpose.

rules.title: Handle failures honestly
rules.section: Keep Persistence Behind Repository Contracts
rules.applies: Storage, network or business work fails
rules.rule: Do not silently claim success; preserve user input and expose a recoverable error when required.
rules.why: The user needs to know whether an operation succeeded.
rules.example: An unsuccessful durable save leaves the editor available for retry.
rules.verify: Inject failures and verify displayed outcomes and state.

rules.title: Keep the dependency flow explicit
rules.section: Layered Architecture
rules.applies: Designing or reviewing application structure
rules.rule: Keep the relationship View → ViewModel → Feature → Microservices; AppModel composes and exposes Features.
rules.why: Dependencies follow clear ownership instead of scattered business decisions.
rules.example: A screen ViewModel asks a schedule Feature, which calls a networking microservice.
rules.verify: Trace a user operation through each layer and inspect reverse dependencies.

rules.title: Coordinate without unnecessary layers
rules.section: Coordinated Application Flow
rules.applies: Implementing a feature workflow
rules.rule: Keep the cooperating parts connected by clear responsibilities and avoid bypassing the Feature that owns a business action.
rules.why: The execution path remains understandable and testable.
rules.example: A refresh reaches the schedule Feature before its provider.
rules.verify: Trace the entry point, owners, state changes and dependencies.

rules.title: Separate domain and display decisions
rules.section: Separate Domain Decisions from Display Decisions
rules.applies: Formatting or presenting Feature results
rules.rule: Features decide domain meaning; ViewModels translate results for display and Views render them.
rules.why: Business decisions stay reusable across devices.
rules.example: A Feature determines a domain result and the ViewModel prepares its display label.
rules.verify: Inspect calculations and business classification for leaks into Views and ViewModels.

rules.title: Apply CFA governing principles
rules.section: Governing Principles
rules.applies: Building or reviewing a CFA app
rules.rule: Use the governing ownership, Swift Concurrency and readability principles together rather than applying one in isolation.
rules.why: Individual conventions are meaningful only as a coherent architecture.
rules.example: A shared Feature owns state and exposes operations to multiple dedicated ViewModels.
rules.verify: Review Feature boundaries, isolation and the full source principles.

rules.title: Avoid complexity without product value
rules.section: Maintenance over Complexity
rules.applies: Adding an abstraction or migration layer
rules.rule: Keep structures simple enough to understand while preserving real behaviour and safety.
rules.why: Unnecessary layers obscure the system and increase maintenance cost.
rules.example: A small sign-out workflow makes explicit Feature calls instead of adding an event bus.
rules.verify: Identify each layer’s concrete responsibility and remove unjustified duplication.

rules.title: Apply the full conformance checklist
rules.section: Review Checklist
rules.applies: Auditing a CFA implementation
rules.rule: Review the complete checklist against the actual app and report findings with evidence.
rules.why: A single passing rule cannot establish whole-app conformance.
rules.example: An audit checks ViewModel ownership, Feature state and task lifetimes.
rules.verify: Trace each applicable checklist item and distinguish unverified behaviour from passes.

rules.title: Avoid prohibited CFA patterns
rules.section: Prohibited Patterns
rules.applies: Implementing or auditing CFA code
rules.rule: Check the full prohibited-pattern list and its applicable context.
rules.why: Known architecture violations should not survive as isolated exceptions.
rules.example: A View does not receive another screen’s ViewModel.
rules.verify: Search source and target membership, then verify actual usage and tests.

rules.title: Create focused test targets
rules.section: Project Identity
rules.applies: Creating an Xcode project
rules.rule: Create a unit-test target; add a UI-test target only for a specifically requested UI automation scenario.
rules.why: Empty test targets add noise without evidence.
rules.example: A new project has Feature and ViewModel unit tests.
rules.verify: Inspect targets and run the relevant unit tests.

rules.title: Keep the template layout and assets correct
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating or editing the CFA Xcode template
rules.rule: Keep App.swift, the root asset catalog and app resources in their prescribed locations and maintain Xcode navigator references.
rules.why: A template must produce a usable project with the expected structure.
rules.example: A StoreKit configuration stays in App Resources and remains linked from its scheme.
rules.verify: Run the template structure verifier and inspect a generated project.

rules.title: Do not create dumping-ground folders
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Organising files
rules.rule: Use folder names that describe the responsibility of their contents rather than vague catch-all folders.
rules.why: Related implementation remains easy to locate.
rules.example: A networking helper lives with the networking capability rather than a generic Helpers folder.
rules.verify: Inspect folder names and the actual responsibilities of their contents.

rules.title: Apply optional visual defaults only in scope
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Shaping a new app or changing an existing product
rules.rule: Use new-product visual defaults when applicable and preserve existing approved designs during maintenance.
rules.why: An architecture task should not silently redesign an existing product.
rules.example: Do not add a CFA Settings footer to an established app unless the request or workflow calls for it.
rules.verify: Compare UI changes with user instructions and the product design authority.

rules.title: Validate device orientation configuration
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Creating an iOS app or preparing its archive
rules.rule: Declare supported orientations in each configuration and inspect the built or archived Info.plist; honour explicit product choices.
rules.why: A simulator build alone does not prove archive configuration or layout compatibility.
rules.example: A universal app declares appropriate iPhone and iPad orientations.
rules.verify: Build Release for a generic iOS device and inspect the built orientation arrays.

rules.title: Organise extensions and domain types by purpose
rules.section: Make the Architecture Visible in the Folder Structure
rules.applies: Adding Swift extensions or domain values
rules.rule: Follow the specification’s placement rules for extensions and keep domain types with their semantic owner.
rules.why: Related types remain understandable independently of storage representation.
rules.example: A launch snapshot belongs with the launch capability rather than being defined by its database schema.
rules.verify: Review extension and type ownership against the full source section.

rules.title: Keep SwiftUI construction fast
rules.section: Give Every Unique Screen Its Own ViewModel
rules.applies: Constructing a SwiftUI View or ViewModel
rules.rule: Avoid blocking I/O, slow work and asynchronous side effects in initializers and body construction.
rules.why: SwiftUI may construct Views repeatedly and must remain responsive.
rules.example: A ViewModel is initialized cheaply and asks its Feature to start work through a named method.
rules.verify: Inspect initializers and measure slow paths where needed.

rules.title: Retain ViewModel-owned unstructured tasks
rules.section: Make Concurrency Behaviour Honest and Visible
rules.applies: A ViewModel creates an unstructured Task
rules.rule: Retain a named handle per independently managed operation; repeated actions may reuse a task when one execution satisfies them all. Do not coalesce commands that must each take effect, even when their inputs match.
rules.why: Task ownership and shared completion stay visible.
rules.example: Repeated refresh taps return the same active task handle.
rules.verify: Test repeated taps, completion cleanup, cancellation and replacement.

rules.title: Never gate UI on database availability
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Launching when persistence is slow or unavailable
rules.rule: Start required work without blocking navigation or first presentation on a database loading gate.
rules.why: Users can access unaffected capabilities and see honest loading or failure states.
rules.example: The root screen appears while a Feature restores local data.
rules.verify: Test slow and failed storage, navigation and first-frame responsiveness.

rules.title: Keep the SwiftUI App entry point structural
rules.section: Use Application Launch as an Opportunity to Refresh Features
rules.applies: Implementing the SwiftUI App entry point
rules.rule: Keep the App structure focused on scene composition and use the application lifecycle for the synchronous AppModel launch signal.
rules.why: Startup ownership remains independent of any one View.
rules.example: The app delegate invokes AppModel directly before returning from launch.
rules.verify: Inspect the App and delegate and confirm no view task starts the shared launch workflow.
